claim: WD patients have a significantly higher incidence of cholecystitis compared to the general population.
source: In this retrospective clinical study of over 600 WD patients, it was found that they had a significantly higher cholecystitis incidence than the general population.
evidence: The abstract states this finding from a retrospective clinical study of over 600 WD patients.

claim: WD patients with cholecystitis have a poorer prognosis compared to other cholecystitis patients.
source: This, in turn, is associated with a poor prognosis for cholecystitis in these patients.
evidence: The text directly states that WD is associated with poor prognosis for cholecystitis.

claim: c.2333G>T (p.R778L) accounts for 65% of ATP7B mutations in the studied WD patient cohort.
source: Through sequencing DNA samples from 20 patients with WD, we found that c. 2333G>T (p. R778L) accounted for the majority (65%) of the three most common mutations in Chinese, while c. 2804C>T (p. T935M) and c. 2975C>T (p. P992L) were not detected (Figure 1a; Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: DNA sequencing data from 20 WD patients is presented in Figure 1a showing the mutation frequency.

claim: ATP7B deficiency in hepatocytes leads to abnormalities in mitochondrial function and copper metabolism.
source: In hepatocytes, ATP7B deficiency in the trans-Golgi network (TGN) leads to abnormalities in mitochondrial function and copper metabolism, and ultimately to a wide range of liver diseases (Figure 1b; Członkowska et al., 2018; Roberts et al., 2008; Zischka and Lichtmannegger, 2014; Muchenditsi et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: WD patients have lower total bilirubin levels compared to HBV patients.
source: Additionally, a lower total bilirubin and metabolic symptoms of WD patients, a lower risk of hyperglycemia (Cohort 1 and Cohort 2), are observed (Figure 1e, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Clinical statistics presented in Figure 1e show lower total bilirubin in WD patients.

claim: ATP7B knockout in WRL 68 hepatocyte cell lines significantly impairs basal oxygen consumption rate and ATP production capacity.
source: Mitochondrial stress and glycolysis assays revealed that knockout of the ATP7B (ATP7B-KO) in human hepatocyte cell lines WRL 68 significantly impaired the basal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and capacity of ATP production, while the extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) of glycolysis and glycolysis capacity remained unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: Experimental data from mitochondrial stress assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b and c.

claim: Chronic cholecystitis incidence is higher in WD patients (49.51%) compared to HBV patients (9.46%) in Cohort 2.
source: Interestingly, chronic cholecystitis emerged as the most common complication, with a notably higher incidence in WD patients (49.51%) compared to HBV patients (9.46%) in Cohort 2 (Figure 1e).
evidence: Clinical statistics from Cohort 2 presented in Figure 1e.

claim: In cholecystitis patients, the proportion of cases with abnormal white blood cell, neutrophil, and lymphocyte counts is significantly higher when combined with WD.
source: Moreover, in cholecystitis patients, the proportion of cases with abnormal index was significantly higher when combined with WD, which included white blood cell (WBC), neutrophil (NEU), and lymphocyte (LYM) counts (Cohort 3, Figure 1e).
evidence: Clinical data from Cohort 3 shown in Figure 1e.

claim: 57,384 high-quality single transcriptomes were generated from scRNA-seq analysis, with 30,068 cells from WD patients and 27,316 from control patients.
source: 57,384 high-quality single transcriptomes were generated, with 30,068 cells in the group of WD patients (CASE) and 27,316 in the group of liver hemangioma patients (CON).
evidence: Direct statement of scRNA-seq data generation results.

claim: 12 significant cell clusters were identified through automated annotation and manual review in the scRNA-seq analysis.
source: This initial annotation process resulted in the classification and display of 12 significant cell clusters.
evidence: Description of the cell annotation methodology and results.

claim: T and NK lineages are the primary immune cell population, accounting for 56.54% in CASE and 73.55% in CON.
source: Our study observed that T and NK lineages were the primary immune cell population among all the examined samples, accounting for 56.54% in CASE and 73.55% in CON, followed by MPs which constituted 17.33% in CASE and 9.97% in CON (Figure 2f, Figure 2—figure supplement 1e, and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Cell composition data presented in Figure 2f and supplementary materials.

claim: The proportion of mononuclear phagocytes is significantly increased in WD patients (17.33% in CASE vs 9.97% in CON).
source: Our study observed that T and NK lineages were the primary immune cell population among all the examined samples, accounting for 56.54% in CASE and 73.55% in CON, followed by MPs which constituted 17.33% in CASE and 9.97% in CON (Figure 2f, Figure 2—figure supplement 1e, and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Cell composition data from scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Mononuclear phagocytes likely dominate the immune microenvironment remodeling in WD patients.
source: The significant increase in the proportion of MPs and decrease in T and NK cells suggest that MPs likely dominate the immune microenvironment remodeling in WD patients, while lymphocytes play a minor role.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observed changes in cell proportions.

claim: Macrophages are significantly increased in WD patients (25.03% in CASE versus 14.33% in CON).
source: In CASE, there was a significant increase in both macrophages (25.03% in CASE versus 14.33% in CON) and KCs, the resident macrophages in the liver (26.03% in CASE versus 22.96% in CON), suggesting their involvement in promoting hepatic inflammation in metabolic liver disease (Figure 3a; Dixon et al., 2013).
evidence: Cell subtype analysis data shown in Figure 3a with citation to prior literature.

claim: The proportion of NK cells is significantly increased in WD patients (40.97% in CASE and 17.07% in CON).
source: The proportion of NK cells (40.97% and 17.07% in CASE and CON, respectively) and CD4Treg (0.92% and 0.31% in CASE and CON, respectively) was significantly increased in CASE.
evidence: Cell subtype proportion data from scRNA-seq analysis.

claim: Genes encoding complement C1q (C1QA, C1QB, and C1QC) and HLA-DRA are significantly upregulated in WD patients.
source: We found that the expression of genes encoding complement C1q (C1QA, C1QB, and C1QC) and HLA-DRA was significantly upregulated in CASE.
evidence: Differential gene expression analysis of immune cells.

claim: Genes encoding heat shock proteins (HSPA1A, HSPA1B, HSPM1, HSPA6, HSP90AB1, HSPE1, and HSPD1) are markedly downregulated in WD patients.
source: Conversely, the expression of genes encoding heat shock protein (HSPA1A, HSPA1B, HSPM1, HSPA6, HSP90AB1, HSPE1, and HSPD1) was markedly downregulated in CASE (Figure 3c).
evidence: Differential gene expression data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: WD enhances antigen processing and presentation, activation of immune response, and positive regulation of lymphocyte activation.
source: The Gene Ontology (GO) analysis results demonstrate that WD enhances the abilities of antigen-presenting cells to activate immune response and related lymphocytes, through upregulating antigen processing and presentation, activation of immune response, and positive regulation of lymphocyte activation.
evidence: GO enrichment analysis results on differentially expressed genes.

claim: CD8Teff, KCs, NKT, CD8MAIT, monocytes, cDC2, and macrophage are the primary participants in intercellular communication.
source: Our findings reveal that CD8Teff, KCs, NKT, CD8MAIT, monocytes, cDC2, and macrophage were the primary participants in intercellular communication, with the high value in both incoming and outgoing interaction strength (Figure 3e).
evidence: CellChat analysis results shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Macrophages_3 subtype in WD patients displays elevated expression of S100A family genes (S100A8, S100A9, S100A12, S100A6, VCAN, FCN1, and S100A4).
source: Macrophages_3 in CASE displayed elevated expression levels of S100A family genes (S100A8, S100A9, S100A12, S100A6, VCAN, FCN1, and S100A4), indicating a potential contribution to MDSC-like macrophages.
evidence: Gene expression analysis of macrophage subtypes.

claim: Macrophages_4 subtype in WD patients is characterized by upregulation of lipid metabolism genes (FABP5, APOC1, CTSD, and PLA2G7).
source: In contrast, Macrophages_4 in CASE were characterized by upregulation of lipid metabolism genes (FABP5, APOC1, CTSD, and PLA2G7) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b; Zhang et al., 2019a; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: Gene expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b with citations.

claim: Macrophages_3 subtype exhibits a more pronounced pro-inflammatory signal in WD patients.
source: Significantly, the Macrophages_3 subtype exhibited a more pronounced pro-inflammatory signal in CASE, while the other subtypes showed a slight decrease.
evidence: Gene signature scoring analysis of macrophage subtypes.

claim: All Kupffer cell subtypes in WD patients show varying degrees of increase in pro-inflammatory and interferon-responsive signatures.
source: Similarly, KCs subtypes in two groups also showed overlapping M1/M2 signatures, but all subtypes in CASE showed varying degrees of increase in pro-inflammatory and interferon-responsive signatures (Figure 4b).
evidence: Gene signature scoring data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Neutrophils in WD patients show decreased maturation, chemotaxis, phagocytosis, and chemokine activity scores.
source: The results showed that the maturation, chemotaxis, phagocytosis, and chemokine activity scores were decreased in CASE, while the activation of the type I interferon signaling pathway was enhanced (Figure 4c).
evidence: Functional scoring analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Genes encoding MHC class I molecules (HLA-A, -B, -C, -E, and -F) are significantly upregulated in mature DCs in WD patients.
source: Notably, genes encoding MHC class I molecules (HLA-A, -B, -C, -E, and -F) were significantly upregulated in the mature DCs in CASE, while genes encoding MHC class II molecules (HLA-DQA1, -DQA2, -DQB1, -DQB2, -DPA1, -DPB1, -DRA, -DRB1, and -DRB5) were all downregulated in the mature DCs.
evidence: Gene expression analysis of dendritic cell subtypes.

claim: Genes encoding MHC class II molecules are downregulated in mature DCs in WD patients.
source: Notably, genes encoding MHC class I molecules (HLA-A, -B, -C, -E, and -F) were significantly upregulated in the mature DCs in CASE, while genes encoding MHC class II molecules (HLA-DQA1, -DQA2, -DQB1, -DQB2, -DPA1, -DPB1, -DRA, -DRB1, and -DRB5) were all downregulated in the mature DCs.
evidence: Gene expression analysis of dendritic cell subtypes.

claim: Immunoglobulin genes (IGHD and IGHM) and naïve B cell marker TCL1A are significantly upregulated in B cells in WD patients.
source: Besides, genes encoding MHC molecules were not the top significant DEGs in B cells, while the immunoglobulin genes (IGHD and IGHM) and the naïve B cell marker TCL1A were significantly upregulated in CASE (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Gene expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e.

claim: S100A8, S100A9, and S100A12 are the top 3 upregulated genes in classical monocytes of WD patients.
source: Compared to CON, S100A8, S100A9, and S100A12 were the top 3 upregulated genes in classical monocytes of CASE (Figure 4—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: Differential gene expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1g.

claim: S100A8 and S100A9 play vital roles in modulating inflammatory responses by recruiting leukocytes and inducing cytokine secretion during inflammation.
source: S100A8 and S100A9 are confirmed to play vital roles in modulating the inflammatory responses by recruiting leukocytes and inducing cytokine secretion during inflammation, and as an alarmin, their elevation indicates inflammation in the local environment (Wang et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2023).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Biological processes linked to energy and lipid metabolism are upregulated in several T cell subtypes in WD patients.
source: Notably, the biological processes linked to energy and lipid metabolism were upregulated in several subtypes, including CD4Tmem_CD40LG, CD4Treg_CTLA4, CD8MAIT_KLRB1, CD8MAIT_SLC4A10, CD8Teff_GZMH, and CD8Teff_GZMK.
evidence: GO enrichment analysis results on T cell subtypes.

claim: NK cell-mediated cytotoxicity, NF-kappa B signaling pathway, and chemokine signaling pathway are downregulated in NK cells of WD patients.
source: The Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) analysis of DEGs in NK cells between CASE and CON revealed downregulation of the NK cell-mediated cytotoxicity, along with the NF-kappa B signaling pathway and chemokine signaling pathway, in CASE (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: KEGG pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Biological processes of oxidative phosphorylation and ATP metabolic process are upregulated in NK cells of WD patients.
source: Interestingly, GO analysis showed upregulated biological processes of oxidative phosphorylation and ATP metabolic process, implying the altered metabolic program in NK cells and immune microenvironment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: KLRC1 and TIGIT expression is significantly upregulated in NK cells of WD patients.
source: The results showed significantly upregulated expression in KLRC1 and TIGIT, and significantly downregulated expression in FCGR3A, TNF, IFNG, GZMB, GNLY, and CCL4 (Figure 5a).
evidence: Gene expression comparison data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: FCGR3A, TNF, IFNG, GZMB, GNLY, and CCL4 expression is significantly downregulated in NK cells of WD patients.
source: The results showed significantly upregulated expression in KLRC1 and TIGIT, and significantly downregulated expression in FCGR3A, TNF, IFNG, GZMB, GNLY, and CCL4 (Figure 5a).
evidence: Gene expression comparison data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: KLRC1 and TIGIT are inhibitory receptors expressed on NK cell surface, and their activation inhibits NK cell functions.
source: KLRC1 and TIGIT are inhibitory receptors expressed on NK cell surface, and their activation inhibits NK cell functions (Zhang et al., 2018; André et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: WD patients have NK cells with exhausted status, which results in poor effector function.
source: It was collectively indicated that WD patients have NK cells with exhausted status, which results in poor effector function.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple lines of gene expression and functional data.

claim: NK cells in WD patients differentiate toward cell fate 2, which represents a more exhausted state.
source: Most of the NK cells in CON differentiated toward cell fate 1, while those in CASE displayed a higher tendency for differentiation toward cell fate 2, with cell grouping occurring at the final stage (Figure 5—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1f.

claim: KLRC1 gene expression gradually increases along the differentiation path to cell fate 2.
source: The results showed that the gene expression of KLRC1 (included in gene cluster 1) was gradually increased along the way to cell fate 2, while the gene expression of FCGR3A, TNF, and GZMB (included in gene cluster 3) was weakened in the same direction, suggesting that cell fate 2 is a more exhausted state of NK cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1g, see full gene list in Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Pseudotime analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1g.

claim: T-bet (encoded by TBX21) gene expression is downregulated in NK cells of WD patients.
source: We found that the gene expression of T-bet (encoded by TBX21) was downregulated and Eomes (encoded by EOMES) was upregulated in CASE (Figure 5—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: PYSCENIC analysis results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1h.

claim: Eomes (encoded by EOMES) gene expression is upregulated in NK cells of WD patients.
source: We found that the gene expression of T-bet (encoded by TBX21) was downregulated and Eomes (encoded by EOMES) was upregulated in CASE (Figure 5—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: PYSCENIC analysis results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1h.

claim: T-bet expression is downregulated in exhausted NK cells, whereas Eomes expression is increased.
source: Consistent with previous studies, T-bet expression was downregulated in exhausted NK cells, whereas Eomes expression was increased (Sun et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022; da Silva et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: KLRC1+ cells are more frequently observed in NK cells in liver tissue sections of WD patients.
source: The mIHC results indicated that KLRC1+ cells were more frequently observed in NK cells marked by CD56 in the liver tissue sections of WD patients (Figure 5b).
evidence: Multiplex immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The percentage of KLRC1+ NK cells is significantly increased in peripheral blood of WD patients.
source: The results showed a significant increase in the percentage of KLRC1+ and TIGIT+ NK cells and a significant decrease in the percentage of IFNγ+ NK cells in peripheral blood lymphocytes from WD patients (Figure 5d).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The percentage of TIGIT+ NK cells is significantly increased in peripheral blood of WD patients.
source: The results showed a significant increase in the percentage of KLRC1+ and TIGIT+ NK cells and a significant decrease in the percentage of IFNγ+ NK cells in peripheral blood lymphocytes from WD patients (Figure 5d).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The percentage of IFNγ+ NK cells is significantly decreased in peripheral blood of WD patients.
source: The results showed a significant increase in the percentage of KLRC1+ and TIGIT+ NK cells and a significant decrease in the percentage of IFNγ+ NK cells in peripheral blood lymphocytes from WD patients (Figure 5d).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The proportion of NK cells in lymphocytes from peripheral blood is significantly higher in WD patients.
source: The significantly higher proportion of NK cells in WD patients was consistent with the scRNA-seq data, and more CD56Bright NK cells suggested a relatively weaker effector function in WD patients (Figure 5—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1i.

claim: WD patients have more CD56Bright NK cells, suggesting relatively weaker effector function.
source: The significantly higher proportion of NK cells in WD patients was consistent with the scRNA-seq data, and more CD56Bright NK cells suggested a relatively weaker effector function in WD patients (Figure 5—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1i with inference about function.

claim: NK cell exhaustion is correlated with poor liver cancer prognosis.
source: There is evidence demonstrating that NK cell exhaustion is correlated with poor liver cancer prognosis (Sun et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A prognostic model based on 12 genes (KLRC1, TIGIT, HAVCR2, PDCD1, CD96, LAG3, FCGR3A, NCR3, NCR2, NCR1, KLRK1, and PRF1) has good prognostic performance for cholecystitis, pancreatitis, lung adenocarcinoma, and hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: Using stepwise regression analysis, 12 genes, KLRC1, TIGIT, HAVCR2, PDCD1, CD96, LAG3, FCGR3A, NCR3, NCR2, NCR1, KLRK1, and PRF1, were selected to obtain the best model. The results showed that the predictive model constructed from these genes had good prognostic performance, with AUC of 0.77, 0.80, 0.97, 0.90 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: Machine learning model construction and ROC analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a–d.

claim: TIGIT is a risk gene (HR>1) for cholecystitis prognosis.
source: Univariate Cox regression analysis revealed that the TIGIT (in GSE166915) and PDCD1 (in GSE75037) were risk genes with hazard ratio (HR)>1, while NCR2 (in GSE91035), HAVCR2, KLRC1, NCR3 (in GSE75037), NCR3, LAG3 (in GSE41804) were protective gene with HR<1 among 12 differently expressed markers of NK cell exhaustion (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: Univariate Cox regression analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a–d.

claim: Patients with high markers of NK cell exhaustion have shorter survival time compared to those with low markers in cholecystitis (p=6.1e-6).
source: Consistently, the Kaplan-Meier survival curves suggested a shorter survival time in the group with high markers of NK cell exhaustion than in the group with low markers in the GSE166915 (p=6.1e-6), GSE91035 (p=1.9e-5), GSE75037 (p=3.8e-16), and GSE41804 (p=3.0e-3) datasets (Figure 6a–d).
evidence: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Patients with high markers of NK cell exhaustion have shorter survival time compared to those with low markers in pancreatitis (p=1.9e-5).
source: Consistently, the Kaplan-Meier survival curves suggested a shorter survival time in the group with high markers of NK cell exhaustion than in the group with low markers in the GSE166915 (p=6.1e-6), GSE91035 (p=1.9e-5), GSE75037 (p=3.8e-16), and GSE41804 (p=3.0e-3) datasets (Figure 6a–d).
evidence: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Patients with high markers of NK cell exhaustion have shorter survival time compared to those with low markers in lung adenocarcinoma (p=3.8e-16).
source: Consistently, the Kaplan-Meier survival curves suggested a shorter survival time in the group with high markers of NK cell exhaustion than in the group with low markers in the GSE166915 (p=6.1e-6), GSE91035 (p=1.9e-5), GSE75037 (p=3.8e-16), and GSE41804 (p=3.0e-3) datasets (Figure 6a–d).
evidence: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Patients with high markers of NK cell exhaustion have shorter survival time compared to those with low markers in hepatocellular carcinoma (p=3.0e-3).
source: Consistently, the Kaplan-Meier survival curves suggested a shorter survival time in the group with high markers of NK cell exhaustion than in the group with low markers in the GSE166915 (p=6.1e-6), GSE91035 (p=1.9e-5), GSE75037 (p=3.8e-16), and GSE41804 (p=3.0e-3) datasets (Figure 6a–d).
evidence: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Wilson's disease is a rare genetic disorder caused by mutations in the gene encoding the transmembrane copper-transporting P-type ATPase protein.
source: Wilson's disease (WD) is a rare genetic disorder caused by mutations in the gene encoding the transmembrane copper-transporting P-type ATPase protein (Bandmann et al., 2015).
evidence: Definition of WD supported by citation.

claim: WD leads to deficits in mitochondrial structure and function, as well as specific alterations in liver metabolism.
source: It leads to deficits in mitochondrial structure and function, as well as specific alterations in liver metabolism, resulting in a variety of liver diseases.
evidence: Description of WD pathophysiology.

claim: WD is commonly associated with inflammatory conditions in the clinic.
source: Additionally, WD is commonly associated with inflammatory conditions in the clinic (Huster et al., 2006; Medici et al., 2013; Huster, 2014; Aggarwal and Bhatt, 2020).
evidence: Clinical observation supported by citations.

claim: NK cells are the major innate lymphocyte subset and are found in most organs.
source: Natural killer (NK) cells are the major innate lymphocyte subset and are found in most organs (Abel et al., 2018; Crinier et al., 2020).
evidence: General statement about NK cells supported by citations.

claim: NK cells produce lytic granules that eliminate infected or cancerous cells, coordinate the inflammation process, form immunological memory, and modulate antigen-presenting cell function in inflammatory diseases.
source: They produce lytic granules that eliminate infected or cancerous cells, coordinate the inflammation process, form immunological memory, and modulate antigen-presenting cell function in inflammatory diseases (Highton et al., 2021; Parisi et al., 2017; Earls and Lee, 2020).
evidence: Description of NK cell functions supported by citations.

claim: NK cell exhaustion is characterized by downregulated expression of activating receptors (e.g. NKG2D, FCGR3A), upregulated expression of inhibitory receptors (e.g. KLRC1, PD-1, TIGIT, Tim-3), decreased production of effector cytokines (e.g. IFNγ, GZMB), and impaired cytolytic activity.
source: In the context of tumors and chronic infections, NK cells exhibit an exhausted phenotype, termed NK cell exhaustion, which is characterized by downregulated expression of activating receptors (e.g. NKG2D, FCGR3A), upregulated expression of inhibitory receptors (e.g. KLRC1, PD-1, TIGIT, Tim-3), decreased production of effector cytokines (e.g. IFNγ, GZMB), and impaired cytolytic activity (Bi and Tian, 2017; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Definition of NK cell exhaustion supported by citations.

claim: Blockade of KLRC1 and TIGIT has been shown to reverse NK cell exhaustion and enhance the therapeutic effects of anti-tumor and anti-infective immunotherapies.
source: Recently, blockade of KLRC1 and TIGIT has been shown to reverse NK cell exhaustion and enhance the therapeutic effects of anti-tumor and anti-infective immunotherapies (Zhang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2019b).
evidence: Statement about therapeutic interventions supported by citations.

claim: The liver contains a substantial population of diverse immune cells, particularly NK cells.
source: It contains a substantial population of diverse immune cells, particularly NK cells (Crispe, 2009; Kubes and Jenne, 2018; Racanelli and Rehermann, 2006).
evidence: Statement about liver immune composition supported by citations.

claim: Liver pathologies affect mesenchymal immune cell function and influence systemic inflammatory responses, impacting the development and outcome of inflammation-associated diseases such as cholecystitis.
source: Furthermore, liver pathologies affect mesenchymal immune cell function and influence systemic inflammatory responses, impacting the development and outcome of inflammation-associated diseases such as cholecystitis (Armstrong et al., 2014; Matyas et al., 2021; Knab et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about liver pathology effects supported by citations.

claim: Systemic inflammation is widely recognized as a primary catalyst of cholecystitis pathology.
source: While the corresponding pathological mechanisms of cholecystitis are complicated, systemic inflammation is widely recognized as a primary catalyst of cholecystitis pathology (Huffman and Schenker, 2010; Markaki et al., 2021; Laurila et al., 2005; Fu et al., 2022; Abu-Sbeih et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement about cholecystitis pathology supported by citations.

claim: The proportion, gene expression profile, and functional status of immune cells hold significant prognostic value in cholecystitis.
source: Compelling evidence supports that the proportion, gene expression profile, and functional status of immune cells hold significant prognostic value (Buonacera et al., 2022; McKinney et al., 2010; McKinney et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2021; Fridman et al., 2017; Wouters and Nelson, 2018).
evidence: Statement about prognostic value supported by citations.

claim: Metabolic crosstalk in the tumor microenvironment disrupts metabolic and signaling pathways in immune cells, leading to dysfunction.
source: Emerging research indicates that metabolic crosstalk in the tumor microenvironment disrupts metabolic and signaling pathways in immune cells, leading to dysfunction (Hosseini et al., 2022; Park et al., 2023; Yan et al., 2023; Bader et al., 2020; Riera-Domingo et al., 2020).
evidence: Statement about metabolic effects on immune cells supported by citations.

claim: Glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation contribute to maintain the cytotoxic ability and promote expansion of NK cells.
source: Interestingly, glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation contribute to maintain the cytotoxic ability and promote expansion of NK cells (Wu et al., 2020; Poznanski and Ashkar, 2019; O'Brien and Finlay, 2019).
evidence: Statement about NK cell metabolism supported by citations.

claim: Kupffer cells are liver-resident macrophages that represent the most abundant population of tissue-resident macrophages in the human body.
source: Kupffer cells, which are liver-resident macrophages with unique functions in maintaining homeostasis, represent the most abundant population of tissue-resident macrophages in the human body (Dixon et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement about Kupffer cells supported by citation.

claim: Elevated CD4 regulatory T cells are correlated with reduced CD8 T cells in WD patients.
source: CD4 regulatory T cells are thought to inhibit T cell activation in autoimmune and virus-related liver diseases, indicating a correlation between elevated CD4 regulatory T cells and reduced CD8 T cells in WD patients (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement about T cell relationships supported by citation.

claim: Heat shock proteins delivering antigens may be responsible for the downregulation of lymphocytes differentiation and T cell activation.
source: However, heat shock proteins delivering antigens may be responsible for the downregulation of lymphocytes differentiation and T cell activation (Shevtsov and Multhoff, 2016).
evidence: Statement about heat shock protein function supported by citation.

claim: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Anhui University of Traditional Chinese Medicine (approval number 2019AH-32).
source: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Anhui University of Traditional Chinese Medicine (approval number 2019AH-32), and the clinical study design, informed consent, and case report were also approved in the document.
evidence: Statement of ethical approval.
